column6: Every API difference between lls and the Java original needs a recorded justification or a fix: a difference is acceptable only when it adds Nullable, makes something final, or adds a test; otherwise Java's spelling wins

— Run 2026-09-19 on one machine, JDK 25, hand-written (commit before generation) vs generated: 113 rows same, 42 faster, 34 slower; the large regressions (traversals through iterators up to 34x, boxed Int lookups 2.5x) fixed in Baltic Porter's lls policy; the rest tracked separately

A filtered for-comprehension over an ArrayView still allocates: zipWithIndex builds a pair per element and a guard holds the predicate as a function object (checked by OverheadClaimsSuite; the README states it)

Sorting a primitive-backed array throws: DynamicArray[Int].sort() and .sort(ordering) fail with ClassCastException (int[] cast to Object[]) in the generated Sort; Select and ArrayMap's Keys/Values toArray carry the same cast. Java's code treats every T[] as Object[], which stopped being true when the generated arrays became primitive-backed. No test covers it (the hand-written lls sorted Int arrays fine). Fix belongs in Baltic Porter's lls policy: box into a temporary Object[] around the sort for a non-reference array, and add tests here

Generated vs hand-written lls, same machine and JDK 25 (2026-09-19): after the traversal and lookup fixes in the lls policy the large-size rows are on par, but some small-size rows remain slower: ObjectMap.foreachEntry 2.4x, OrderedSet.foreach 2.2x, OrderedMap.foreachEntry 1.7x at 100 elements; Int contains/indexOf/removeValue 1.6-2.0x at 10000 elements; OrderedMap.get 2.2x at 100 keys. 42 rows are faster than the hand-written version
